utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. This morning we sit to hear by videolink the balance of evidence of a witness. There are various witness protections in place so that the witness is to be heard under a pseudonym and with voice and face distortion among other matters. I will speak to the Court Officer in Belgrade. The witness is ready now, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours, that's correct, the witness is in the waiting room, and he is ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am, sorry, we were not able to hear you then. Could you repeat what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, good morning, Your Honours, the witness is ready to testify, and he is in the waiting room. And I'm ready it to bring him upon your direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating that again, we are having trouble getting the right sound balance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours, I hope I'm getting through loud and clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And again.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] good morning, Your Honours, I hope I'm getting through loud and clear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that's coming better now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honours. And the witness is ready to testify. He is in the waiting room, and I can escort him in once Your Honours so direct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could do that now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Witness. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not hearing the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you read that out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now, if you would just pause a moment and we will speak to counsel. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a technical problem with the interpretation for the accused. The accused is not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have found you need full volume on the red for the communication from Belgrade, and then separately a reduced volume on the in-court. Would the interpreters please continue their interpretation of what I am now saying to try and assist. And we have now been introduced a hum from some further microphone, which has been introduced into the circuit just to add to the technical difficulties. We appear now to have sound in the courtroom in B/C/S, but we do have that additional hum that has been introduced during that exercise. Well, we will proceed now. Now, Mr. Behar, are there any problems with you at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Not thus far, Your Honour. I was, I thought, having some difficulty receiving the interpretation on the red channel, but I'm hoping it will be fine, and I'll certainly let you know if I have any problems going forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, witness, thank you for that. We are getting the technicalities adjusted so that we can be sure to both hear and see you and receive interpretation. We think those matters are now corrected and what the Chamber will do is first of all ask Mr. Behar if he has any additional questions for you. And we'll do that now. Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I thought I would address the Chamber very briefly just to set out what I plan to do in brief this morning. I had proposed to first have the witness confirm his identity, then read in a brief witness summary as we normally do with 92 ter witnesses. And I do propose just to have a couple of very brief questions, and I do understand that the purpose of this is really primarily for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Behar. As you will recall, when the witness was unable to attend much earlier in the trial, the Chamber received the statement of the witness that he is now available primarily for cross-examination. Therefore, if you could proceed as you propose quickly, we can move to cross-examination very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I wanted to begin by having you look briefly at a document that contains some personal information related to you. If you could look at P1417. I believe it should be the last tab in the materials that you have there. Have you found that material, sir?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just read that quietly to yourself. Sir, is the information on that document, your name and your date and place of birth correct?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I would note that that has already been made a sealed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And just a reminder now, sir, I will be referring to you as K87 today in order to protect your identity. We are also making use of image and voice distortion. Sir, I can indicate to you and to the Chamber that there are several materials relating to your evidence that are already admitted in evidence, and this was pursuant to this Chamber's order of the 28th of October of 2009. There's your witness statement through this Tribunal, that's P1414. There's a redacted version of your witness statement, that's P1415. There's a transcript of your testimony from the Milutinovic case, that's P1416. There's the pseudonym sheet that you just referred to, that's P1417. And there's also a supplemental information sheet for changes that you had provided or new things you had said to the Prosecution when you testified in Milutinovic case, and that's D392.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would now proceed to read a brief summary of the witness's evidence. K87 is a Serb who was employed as a MUP officer during the time in question. In 1996, he was assigned to the SAJ and based in Batajnica near Belgrade at the 13 Maj training centre. He describes the structure and layout of the 13 Maj training centre, noting that the SAJ left the 13 Maj centre for a period of time after the war started. The witness explains that he received a telephone call from Vlastimir Djordjevic sometime around mid-April of 1999. Mr. Djordjevic directed him to go to his office the following morning, where the two of them met alone. Mr. Djordjevic directed him to facilitate the burial of a large number of human bodies that were contained in trucks that had been driven to the 13 Maj centre. Mr. Djordjevic gave him specific directions as to where and how to bury the bodies. The witness and another MUP officer participated in burying the bodies, as directed by Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Djordjevic contacted the witness on several more occasions, and the witness facilitated the burial of more bodies. He was contacted by telephone by another person after these burials, who asked him to confirm that the bodies were buried. The witness later advised the commander of the SAJ the bodies were being buried at the centre. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to ask you a couple of very brief questions and then counsel for Mr. Djordjevic will have certainly many more questions for you. Sir, were you familiar with Radovan Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And did you attend his funeral?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Was Mr. Trajkovic at that funeral as well?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: He was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And did you speak to him, to Mr. Trajkovic at the funeral?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall how long after Mr. Aleksic's death that funeral took place?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Whose death? Whose funeral? The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sure. I'm just trying to get a sense, sir, if you remember when that funeral was?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: You are asking me if I know the date when Mr. Aleksic was buried, is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's correct. What date was that funeral, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Do you recall how long after Mr. Aleksic's death the funeral took place? Was there a long delay between the time when he died and when the funeral took place, or was it relatively fast?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Not too much time passed, but I'm not sure. What does that mean, was he buried quickly? I don't know. Do you mean was the funeral itself quick? I don't know. The questions are put in such a way that I don't really understand them all that well. Does that mean -- what does it mean, was the burial or the funeral held quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I was just trying to get a sense, sir, of how long after the death of Mr. Aleksic his funeral took place. I think you've answered that already. You've said not too much time passed. Does that sound correct, sir? Do you understand what I'm asking now?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I understand. And I think that, yes, not too much time passed. I don't know exactly how much time, but not a lot, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, those are my questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Behar. Now, the Chamber will ask Mr. Popovic who represents the accused man Mr. Djordjevic, if he has some questions for you. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence -- in view of the health of the witness, the Defence will do its best to keep its cross-examination as short as possible, and that is why I'm going to ask (redacted) to answer my questions and I'm not going to put more questions to him then essential. I apologise, I said the name. I should have used the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a redaction made, Mr. Popovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. K87, I'm Alexander Popovic, and I'm in Mr. Djordjevic's Defence team. I would like to put some questions to you. First of all, I would like to ask you this, we speak the same language so I would like you to listen to my question first and then a little bit after that give your answer so that we can help the interpreters to do their job properly. Sir, Mr. K87, I'm interested in the following, this is a part of your statement that you gave to the Prosecution, paragraph 15, where you refer to a meeting, and you say, The meeting with Djordjevic was very brief and nobody else attended except for us, he told me that this is something that should not be talked about and that we should wait for the war to finish. Witness, I'm going to ask you to pay attention to this conversation you had with Mr. Djordjevic. First of all, are you thinking of the first conversation that you had with Mr. Djordjevic here?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, the first conversation that I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me where the conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: It -- can I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, go ahead, please do.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: The NATO bombing was underway, the NATO bombing of Serbia, so all the important facilities were relocated. The MUP was in the Komercijalna Banka or invest -- or Belgrade Bank. I don't know which one of those banks it was located in. But in any case, it was relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the MUP was located somewhere, do you know who was where in that period? Who was in which location?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: As far as I know, the MUP leadership was transferred there. Relocated, not transferred actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you turned up for this meeting, this conversation, what did the room look like from what you can recall where you had this conversation with Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, it was just a regular office. Just a regular clerk's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the conversation began, can you tell me how it proceeded, what was it like. Briefly can you tell us what you remember of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, it's been a long time since that meeting. I really do not remember all the details, but I can just tell you approximately how the meeting proceeded. I was summoned to the meeting. I went inside. I found Mr. Djordjevic inside who at that time was walking around the office and he was speaking on the telephone with somebody. When he finished his conversation, he spoke to me. And that's what it looked like more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we be a little bit more precise now. I'm going to put questions to you now that have to do with that conversation. When you say he was walking around the office, can you please tell me what was your impression? What was his physical and mental state at the time? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: At the time I had the impression that he was irritable, nervous, and thoughtful, this is the impression that I had. Perhaps I'm not correct, but that was the impression that I had, that he was thinking and that he was nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And when he addressed you, do you remember what he told you? How did he explain to you what you were supposed to do? Can you be a little bit more precise about that, please.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Of course. The General told me that there is a task that had to be completed, that it was our duty to do that. Then he told me what it was and that this was a job that had to be completed. These people had to be buried. They came from the NATO bombing and that at that point in time it was not desirable to talk about it, that it was necessary to wait until the end of the war to be able to then do the identification of the individuals and bury them individually and that it was important throughout the time that this was being done there should be some kind of marking so that there was a trail indicating what was done and where it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: K87, sir, when you were told that there should be some kind of trail or marking left, did you actually act upon that? Did you fulfill that condition?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, of course we did. What Mr. Djordjevic told me was that there was some kind of instruction that this had to be marked and preserved that -- so that there is a record of where we left what we left, so that's what we did. We left a trailer truck there, that was the most convenient thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you leave this trailer truck?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, it was left and for the sole purpose of marking the place so that when the time came to bury the corpses -- rebury the corpses, we would know exactly where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this was the assignment given to you by Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes. I was the only one who was in contact with Mr. Djordjevic. My only contact was with him, so it was natural that this then had come from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you talked with Mr. Djordjevic about this assignment, I don't mean about marking the place, but generally this assignment that you were given, how did he -- how did you understand that? Was that his direct order or was he conveying somebody else's order to you?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: The General was speaking in the plural. Now, what does that mean, speaking in the plural? We should carry out this task. So on the basis of that if I'm supposed to draw a conclusion, the only one I can draw is that someone had told him that, had said that. That's to say that I had the impression -- I mean, I repeat, if he was speaking, he was speak in the plural, and then I feel that he was conveying someone's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did he mention anyone during that conversation as someone who could have issued that order? Did you draw any conclusion in that regard?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, the General never mentioned anybody's name or surname, that this was being done on someone's instructions. However, at one moment, now was it then or, I don't know, the time after that when we saw each other, he mentioned someone who he probably knew; I didn't. He mentioned a nickname, he said the boss, the boss. So I don't know. I could not say anything more than that. I cannot say who he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted), at that point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a further redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know at that moment who was the immediate superior of Mr. Djordjevic or, rather, who his boss was?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: It was only the minister who could have been the General's boss. No one else in the ministry could have been his boss then. He was the number two man in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted), I'm going to ask you now for yet another clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I made a mistake yet again. Again I mentioned the witness's name. Line 19, so could a redaction be made again.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness K87, I would like to ask you to have a look at paragraph 25 of your statement. In that statement you speak about your second meeting with Mr. Djordjevic and you say: "At one moment I talked to Djordjevic in his office and I asked him whether it was possible to stop the bringing of bodies to the centre." Witness, my question has to do with this second meeting. Could you explain in a bit more detail, if you remember, of course, how that conversation evolved? Where it took place, and also could you tell us more specifically what it was that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: The essence of the conversation is what I put here in the statement. Now, I will try, of course, to remember some details as well to the best of my ability now, as much as I can remember. As for this event that had taken place, we talked about it at the same place where I was summoned to have my first meeting with Mr. Djordjevic. And, of course, I asked Mr. Djordjevic if it was possible not to have these bodies brought in again to Batajnica. And, of course, Mr. Djordjevic did show his understanding in view of my proposal. He said, of course, he would have to look into the matter with someone. And generally speaking, as far as he was concerned, his reaction was favourable in relation to my proposal and my idea. His reaction was a favourable one, and it was my understanding that it was a gesture of his goodwill to be accommodating and that he approved what I said. And after that, of course, bodies were no longer brought to the centre in Batajnica. And that is what I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. During your conversation with Mr. Djordjevic -- or actually, let's put it this way: In relation to what you told us just now, I would like to hear about your impression. When you talked to Mr. Djordjevic about putting a stop to the bringing of bodies to Batajnica, what psychological and physical condition was he in? What was his attitude towards all of that?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I think, well, this is going to require an effort on my part. I will have to concentrate. I will have to analyse the General. And on a personal level, I really don't know him, so it would be hard for me to assess our official communication in that way. However, my impression was that everything that was being done was being done against his will. And the impression I had was, Let us hope that this will finally be brought to an end. I'm not saying this in any negative sense. Like, sort of, Let's get rid of this problem, let's take care of this. That was the impression I had during this conversation when I asked him to make an effort to put a stop to having those bodies brought into our centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, during the conversations you had with him, did he ever tell you where these bodies originated from, the ones that were supposed to be buried within the Batajnica compound?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: This is what I was told: I think that in the statement that I gave I did say at one point that they were victims of NATO bombing. I didn't know these people. I was not told at any point in time that they were Serbs or Albanians or gypsies or whatever. Now, I think that that is how the conversation evolved, and our conversations did not involve a great many detail. And I was not in a position to put some kind of questions to the General or whatever. I assumed that everybody understands that, what my position was. I mean, what it's like when you talk to such a high-ranking MUP official, as General Djordjevic was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When he said to you that it was a state secret, as you said in your statement --

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what your understanding was of that. At that moment, I mean.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, like any normal person, there was a state of war in Serbia then. There was marshall law, and it was my understanding that it was only natural that something could be declared a secret, and it was my understanding, the explanation I received was that this would be the situation only until the NATO bombing was still on, and while the war was still on. Afterwards, the corpses would be taken care of. However, during that state of war, while these laws are in force, it was my understanding that it was a state secret then. It wasn't a state secret to conceal the event as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: At that moment was that quite normal and acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: For anyone it would have been normal then. Why would I be any exception to that? That's the situation that we were in then. That was the state that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, witness, K87. The next thing I would like to ask you about is document P413. That is entitled "Official Note," and the date is the 22nd of June, 2001. At the end of this document it says the note was compiled by the Working Group. Witness K87, my question, first of all, is whether you made a statement on the 22nd of June, 2001, and if so, to whom.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date. I cannot say specifically whether it was on the 21st or whatever the date was. I then had an informal exchange of views or exchange of information, conversation with a man who was in charge of talking to me then, and that was Mr. Dragan Karleusa. We talked in the MUP, on MUP premises. Before that we had a telephone contact at my insistence. I came to his office, and we talked about the event that had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness K87, was any kind of statement compiled then and did you sign any statement then?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, no statement was made. No one was taking notes. I didn't sign anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at this exhibit which is before you, I assume, tell me, when did you first see this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Well, when I was preparing -- when I first testified. I mean in the Milutinovic case, I think it was then.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: 2007, I think. Or 2008. I don't know exactly when I was there. I mean, I have been trying to clear my mind of all of these things that had happened, so I really don't know which year I came to testify in the Milutinovic case, was it 2007, was it 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of June, 2001. And then from then up until that year, 2007 or 2008, you never saw this Official Note; right?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I did not. I think it was then when I was preparing for my testimony that I first saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps it's a bit superfluous, but I have to ask you whether before that you ever had occasion to read this Official Note?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, no. No one ever presented it to me and no one ever gave it to me to read, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness K87, while you were preparing to testify in the Milutinovic case and while you were preparing to testify today, did you have an opportunity to read this?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: A bit later I'm going to deal with a large part of this statement, but this is what I'm primarily interested in. Since you had the opportunity of reading it, and I suppose that you know what it was that you discussed with Mr. Karleusa, does this statement depict the subject of your conversation with Mr. Karleusa?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I have already expressed my views in relation to this statement. During my proofing for the first testimony, I said that, and I stand by that to this day. It is written in a very nice way, in a literary fashion. If I'm supposed to interpret it freely now, I will, but I stand by each and every word I stated then as my view regarding this Official Note. If you have that with you there, you can read it out, and I will confirm that for you. If not, I'm going to provide a free interpretation of it now. It was written up very nicely in literary fashion in order to leave the impression of a well-educated person, eloquent.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read that to you now, what you mentioned to us. First of all, what we received from our colleagues from the OTP is a document containing supplemental information concerning the meeting with you on the 10th of May, 2010, and it says there: "K87 repeats that the statement given to the Working Group of the MUP is not correct. Ninety per cent of it is not correct and that the document is an interpretation provided by Mr. Karleusa." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read out to you what you said when you testified in the Milutinovic case in respect of the same matter. It was on the 15th of March, 2007. The witness stated that this document was Karleusa's interpretation of an informal conversation that he had with him. He stated that there were obvious inaccuracies in the document that he had not signed. In this regard, he does not stand by anything that is stated in that document. Not even by the allegations that may be correct because the document does not fully reflect what it was that he said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with all of this, witness?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, I will have to mention some of the allegations made in the Official Note that had been compiled, and that in a way became an exhibit in this case. On page 1, the following is stated: "Then I telephoned General Vlastimir Djordjevic and I asked him about the specific truck that no one had known anything about. After that, the General phoned me on my mobile phone." Does that correspond to the truth and what you said to Mr. Karleusa?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2, paragraph 1: "General Vlastimir Djordjevic told me that the Kosovo terrain was being cleared and that this should be concealed with us, that this was a secret and that this is some report back to Mr. Milosevic about that." Did you ever discuss anything to that effect with Mr. Karleusa?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I did speak with Mr. Karleusa, but this does not reflect the truth. Something like this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There is a sentence in the same paragraph: "When I receive the order from General Djordjevic, I informed my superiors Simovic and Trajkovic about this who happened to be in Kosovo at the time." Does this correspond to the truth as to what you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, this does not correspond to the truth of what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, paragraph number 5: "After that the job became a routine one. Lipovac would inform me by telephone usually saying, It's arriving tonight." Does this correspond to what was said in this informal conversation?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: There are a few other allegations here. First of all you say: "I personally never waited for any truck when it came with the corpses. And after the first batch, I would usually inform Lipovac personally about the assignment." Does this correspond to the truth?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I didn't manage to find that. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is page 2, last sentence in the one paragraph but last: "I personally did not wait for any truck that would arrive with the bodies. And after the first batch, I would personally inform Lipovac about the completion of the assignment."

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: This is absolutely untrue. 50/50. I never did wait for any truck, yes, that is true. But it's absolutely untrue that I informed about the assignment this person whose name you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm particularly interested in and even though you explained that and you said that this wasn't true, I'm still going to put questions to you about that. Did General Vlastimir Djordjevic mention the clearing of terrain in Kosovo to you at any time, and did you ever mention that in your conversation with Mr. Karleusa?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, no. The General never mentioned that to me, anything like that. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more thing, the need to inform President Milosevic, did Mr. Djordjevic in his conversation with you ever refer to President Milosevic, and did you ever refer to him in your conversation with Mr. Karleusa?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: No, the General never mentioned anybody's last name. Absolutely not Milosevic's. And I never said anything like that to Mr. Karleusa. I'm stating this emphatically. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I'm going to ask you for one more clarification. I'm going to quote to you from the last paragraph on page 3 of your statement, where it is said: "My commanders Simovic and Trajkovic I took to the location where the bodies were buried and showed it to them so that they would know in the event of possible future plans about any works that might be carried out on this location." Did you say anything to this effect to Mr. Karleusa, and did you take Simovic and Trajkovic to this location?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I never said anything like this. And I did not take either of my commanders, Mr. Simovic or Mr. Trajkovic to any location. And this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: After all of your answers I still need to ask you this, witness, K87: Can you assume or do you know when you look at this Official Note and everything that is written there, how do you explain all the facts that are mentioned there if you say that that is something that you never said?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I never paid any particular attention to this statement. I never really carefully analysed it in the way that we have just done at your prompting. We analysed it and went detail by detail through it, and the impression that I get, it doesn't have to be the correct impression, is that it is full of untruths, that it is quite pretentious, and that there are indications that certain things are being ascribed to the General. This is something that one can conclude. I am, I repeat, analysing it like this in more detail for the first time. And this Official Note, it is something that leads me, personally, to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, (redacted). Thank you, Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Popovic. Mr. Behar, is it convenient to continue now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few questions for you arising out of the answers that you've just given. Sir, you testified that in your first meeting with Mr. Djordjevic, he was speaking in the plural, and you said - and this was at page 12 of the transcript for my friend - you said that he referred to someone as "the boss," and then you said "I cannot say who he meant." And you were asked then to speculate about who his boss could have been, and you said "the minister." That was your speculation. Sir, I want to ask you, was anyone else Mr. Djordjevic's boss at that time? Was there anyone else who was senior to him?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: At the ministry only the minister. Mr. Djordjevic was a ministry man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Let's just focus on my question, sir --

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: The number two man in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, sir, was anyone else in the entire chain of command, not just within the ministry, was anyone else senior to Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Only the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: What about Mr. Milosevic, sir, was he senior to Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Milosevic did not command the police. He was in command of the army. He was the Commander-in-Chief. The president of a state is the supreme commander of the army. The police is under the command of the minister. This is what I know, what we have been taught in schools, that this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, but if you can just focus on my question. For now I'm just asking you was Mr. Milosevic senior to Mr. Djordjevic? It's a very straightforward question.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I think not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So you are saying that Mr. Milosevic was not senior to Mr. Djordjevic, he was not capable of giving him an order?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I think that he would not be able to do that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you explain that, sir? Can you explain why not, why you have that view now?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I always thought that the communication is normal, that the president of the state, it doesn't matter who it is, Milosevic or Jankovic, the president of the state would communicate with the minister. He wouldn't communicate with the number two or the number three man in the ministry, but with the number one person, and that is the minister. And that is how it works everywhere in the world. So I really wouldn't know about the details whether Milosevic could issue an order to Djordjevic out of the usual procedure. That is something that I'm not aware of. But I'm telling you what I know from books, what I have been taught, and what I'm obliged to know of the hierarchy of the state that I live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, was Mr. Milosevic senior to Minister Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't know. At the time Mr. Milutinovic was minister of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Well, sir, maybe I'll move off of this topic for a moment. Sir, you were asked about how you knew that a new truck with bodies would be arriving at the centre, and you -- this was when you were going through the statement, the Working Group statement, and you denied that Mr. Lipovac would call you. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that Mr. Lipovac did not call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us how did you learn that a new truck would be arriving at the centre? So if there was a new truck that was coming or that had arrived, how would you be informed about that?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Like I said in the statement that I gave to the investigators, Mr. Djordjevic would inform me about the arrival of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And so would this also be the case when additional trucks were arriving, sir? In other words, after the first truck had arrived?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. This happened on three or four more occasions that we communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you explain how he would inform you or how you would learn that this -- that a new truck was arriving?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Who? Do you mean he -- I don't understand -- the question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I just wanted some additional explanation, sir. You said that Mr. Djordjevic would inform you about the arrival of the truck. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I'm just asking if you can explain how he would inform you.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: By telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And can you tell us when he would call in relation to the truck? Was it before when it was -- was it -- sorry, I'll start again. Was it before the truck had arrived, would he tell you it was coming? Was it after?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: The first time it was after it arrived. And the other times I think it was before it arrived. I don't know exactly. I really cannot say now. But I know that the first time it was once the truck had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Can you explain, sir, what Mr. Lipovac's role was?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: What I know is this: Mr. Lipovac had a logistical technical role. On a couple of occasions he brought fuel which was poured into the trucks and then they were driven off to a direction or destination unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And you say he brought fuel. Can you just explain to us, to the Court, where he brought the fuel to.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know where he loaded the fuel. I know that he would bring it to the centre in Batajnica. The trucks were refueled there and then they were taken somewhere. I don't know where. That was his assignment or his task as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think that answers the question, sir. Thank you. And, sir, do you know what Mr. Lipovac's job was?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: What his professional role was within the ministry? I am more looking for his --

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I don't think that he had any -- I don't know what his professional role was, his title. I know that he was performing the duties of Mr. Djordjevic's driver. I know him as somebody who did those jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, just to very briefly revisit some question I'd asked you earlier. I made a mistake and referred to Minister Milutinovic. Of course, I meant to refer to Minister Stojiljkovic. And maybe I'll just put the question to you again. I'd asked first the simple question, was Mr. Milosevic senior to Minister Stojiljkovic? Can you answer that for us, sir.

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, by his position, of course he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So then, sir, was Mr. Milosevic also senior to Mr. Djordjevic in your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: Yes, by nature of his post, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So -- and I know you've speculated on this, sir, but when Mr. Djordjevic was referring to his boss, could that have been Mr. Milosevic, sir? Or to the boss, I should say, could that have been Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: You are expecting me to give you my opinion or to interpret that freely. Could you please clarify your question so that we can stay in a proper professional conversation until the end so that I would be able to say how it was. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I think my question is clear, sir. You had offered earlier your speculation that that may have been the minister that Mr. Djordjevic was referring to, and I'm asking you when he used the term "the boss," to your knowledge could that have referred to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: K87
utterances.text: I personally think not because a high-ranking police official, I believe, could not afford himself such a luxury to call the president of the republic as boss. I don't think that somebody would do that. That is my personal opinion, that they would not refer to the president of the state as the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Those are my questions for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know, witness, that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would thank you for your attendance in Belgrade to deal with these questions, and indicates that you are now free to go about your ordinary activities. Your evidence to us has reached an end. So we will thank you, and we will close the videolink for today. It will be resumed tomorrow for another reason. So thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I would like to wish everybody a lot of luck and good health, and good-bye to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes the evidence of this witness. If we could close the videolink or the screen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, we have finished very early, much earlier than expected, the evidence of this witness today. Our next witness is programmed to be heard tomorrow at 9.00. Before we adjourn for the day, there are some housekeeping matters that I need to deal with. On the 10th of May, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence that it had received a formal English translation of the document that was marked for identification as P1526. That being so, the Prosecution will have leave to upload that translation, and that having been done, the document will become Exhibit P1526 with the English translation attached to it. Next, on the 11th of May, the Defence notified the Chamber and the Prosecution that it had received English translations of four documents that had been marked for identification as D901, D903, D907, and D908. Those translations may now be uploaded in e-court, and the documents marked for identification with the numbers that I've indicated will now become exhibits with those same numbers. The Chamber has also noted that several transcripts have been admitted in this case pursuant to Rule 92 ter, but when they are checked, the transcripts are not corrected transcripts. They may not contain post-session redactions and other corrections. These are presently Exhibits P428, P495, P979, P1321 and P1416. They are in each case Prosecution exhibits. Accordingly, the Chamber would ask that the transcripts that are in these exhibits be checked and final transcripts that include any corrections and redactions that may have been given in closed or private session should be incorporated. And with those final transcripts incorporated, the exhibits will continue to have the same exhibit number. So that's a homework job for the Prosecution with respect to five of the existing exhibits. We don't have corrected and final transcripts. There's a further matter the Chamber would mention as a practical measure at this time when both parties will be reviewing evidence as they prepare their final submissions. There are many cases in the course of this trial over the last year and three or four months where out of caution the Chamber has heard certain evidence in closed session or in private session when by the end of that questioning it's been clear that there's been no need for the evidence to have been received in private or closed session. It was done out of caution, whether it was a Prosecution or Defence witness, just to be sure that there was no reference to some matter that should not have been publicly referred to. The Chamber proposes before it concludes this case to remove the orders for private or closed session that are unnecessary, as it were, to free up the transcript as much as possible for public record, and to free it up for the purposes of reference to the transcript for purposes of submissions and judgement. We would ask both Prosecution and Defence if, as they are reviewing the transcript, they notice there are passages that are for no good reason the subject of an order for closed or private session, that they bring this to the attention of the Chamber's Legal Officer so that it can be included in a general order that relaxes any unnecessary orders for private and closed session. Is there any other matter that needs attention at this stage, Mr. Behar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see your learned leader behind was getting ready to answer that. He acknowledges the reliability of what you have said. We will in the circumstances then adjourn for the day with a view to resuming tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.21 a.m.
